items.stem: Which of the following best describes "charismatic authority"?
options: A regime in which elections are held but the playing field is tilted so heavily that the incumbent rarely loses (Levitsky and Way)
The right of each of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (China, France, Russia, the UK and the US) to block substantive resolutions
Acceptance by other states and international organizations of a government as the rightful representative of a state
Authority based on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader that inspire devotion (Weber)
items.answer: Authority based on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader that inspire devotion (Weber)
items.markingKey: D. "charismatic authority" is authority based on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader that inspire devotion (Weber).

items.stem: "Charismatic authority only exists in dictatorships." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Democratic leaders can have charismatic authority too, e.g. Barack Obama or Jacinda Ardern; charisma is a basis of authority, not a regime type.
items.markingKey: Democratic leaders can have charismatic authority too, e.g. Barack Obama or Jacinda Ardern; charisma is a basis of authority, not a regime type. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between authority and power.
items.answer: Power is the ability to make others act, including through coercion; authority is power accepted as legitimate, so people comply because they believe they ought to.
items.markingKey: Power is the ability to make others act, including through coercion; authority is power accepted as legitimate, so people comply because they believe they ought to. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"The constitution, not the man, is our protection. Presidents come and go; the court that checks them remains."
— Editorial in a Latin American newspaper, 2022 (adapted)

With reference to the source, identify the type of authority described and explain it.
items.answer: Legal-rational authority: legitimacy comes from constitutional rules and institutions (courts) rather than from individual leaders; office-holders are temporary and constrained.
items.markingKey: Legal-rational authority: legitimacy comes from constitutional rules and institutions (courts) rather than from individual leaders; office-holders are temporary and constrained. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Briefly describe Nelson Mandela and post-apartheid South Africa and explain what it reveals about charismatic and legal-rational authority.
items.answer: After his release in 1990 Mandela led the ANC to victory in 1994 and stepped down after one term in 1999. his personal charisma helped legitimise the new constitutional order, while his voluntary departure strengthened rule-based authority
items.markingKey: Context (After his release in 1990 Mandela led the ANC to victory in 1994 and stepped down after one term in 1999.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: his personal charisma helped legitimise the new constitutional order, while his voluntary departure strengthened rule-based authority – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to charismatic and legal-rational authority.

items.stem: Briefly describe the monarchy of Saudi Arabia and explain what it reveals about traditional authority.
items.answer: The Al Saud dynasty rules as an absolute monarchy whose legitimacy draws on lineage, the alliance with religious authorities and custodianship of the holy mosques of Mecca and Medina. authority rests on dynastic inheritance and religious tradition rather than elections
items.markingKey: Context (The Al Saud dynasty rules as an absolute monarchy whose legitimacy draws on lineage, the alliance with religious authorities and custodianship of the holy mosques of Mecca and Medina.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: authority rests on dynastic inheritance and religious tradition rather than elections – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to traditional authority.

items.stem: Analyse the sources of legitimacy of one political leader or regime you have studied, using both Weber and Beetham.
items.answer: Identify the dominant Weberian type and apply Beetham's legality, shared beliefs and consent; e.g. Modi (electoral, charismatic), Xi Jinping (performance, party-legal), the Taliban (religious-traditional). Judge which source matters most.
items.markingKey: Identify the dominant Weberian type and apply Beetham's legality, shared beliefs and consent; e.g. Modi (electoral, charismatic), Xi Jinping (performance, party-legal), the Taliban (religious-traditional). Judge which source matters most.

items.stem: "Legal-rational authority is the most stable form of legitimacy." How far do you agree? Justify your answer with reference to at least one key concept.
items.answer: Legal-rational authority is generally most stable over time, but it depends on a culture of respect for rules.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rule-based succession (peaceful transfers of power); not dependent on one person. Arguments against: democratic backsliding shows rules can be eroded (Hungary); traditional monarchies have survived for centuries (Japan, Gulf). Supported judgement: Legal-rational authority is generally most stable over time, but it depends on a culture of respect for rules. Markbands (10): 9–10 – focused, balanced argument with specific, accurate examples and a well-supported judgement; 7–8 – relevant examples, counter-claims considered, reasoned judgement; 5–6 – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive, judgement asserted; 3–4 – limited, general knowledge with little evaluation; 1–2 – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Explain why Weber described his three types of authority as "ideal types".
items.answer: They are analytical models; real regimes mix them – e.g. the UK combines traditional monarchy with legal-rational parliamentary government, and leaders may add charisma.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are analytical models; real regimes mix them – e.g. the UK combines traditional monarchy with legal-rational parliamentary government, and leaders may add charisma. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why charismatic authority is often unstable.
items.answer: It rests on one person; when the leader dies or loses appeal, authority must be "routinised" into rules or traditions, or the regime faces a succession crisis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It rests on one person; when the leader dies or loses appeal, authority must be "routinised" into rules or traditions, or the regime faces a succession crisis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between traditional authority and legal-rational authority.
items.answer: Traditional authority rests on custom and inheritance and belongs to a person or dynasty; legal-rational authority rests on impersonal rules and procedures and belongs to an office.
items.markingKey: Traditional authority rests on custom and inheritance and belongs to a person or dynasty; legal-rational authority rests on impersonal rules and procedures and belongs to an office. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the monarchy of Saudi Arabia shows traditional authority.
items.answer: The Al Saud dynasty rules as an absolute monarchy whose legitimacy draws on lineage, the alliance with religious authorities and custodianship of the holy mosques of Mecca and Medina. authority rests on dynastic inheritance and religious tradition rather than elections
items.markingKey: Context (The Al Saud dynasty rules as an absolute monarchy whose legitimacy draws on lineage, the alliance with religious authorities and custodianship of the holy mosques of Mecca and Medina.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: authority rests on dynastic inheritance and religious tradition rather than elections – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to traditional authority.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"He came out of prison and the crowds simply followed him. People trusted him more than any law."
— Recollection of a South African activist, 2014 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, how charismatic authority works.
items.answer: People obey because of their trust in the leader's exceptional personal qualities (moral example after imprisonment) rather than rules or tradition.
items.markingKey: People obey because of their trust in the leader's exceptional personal qualities (moral example after imprisonment) rather than rules or tradition. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that weber's three types of authority remain useful for understanding legitimacy today?
items.answer: Weber's types remain a useful starting point, but must be supplemented by performance and international dimensions of legitimacy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many regimes still fit (Gulf monarchies, constitutional democracies, populist leaders); helps explain stability and succession crises. Arguments against: ignores performance legitimacy (China); neglects international recognition; real cases are mixed. Supported judgement: Weber's types remain a useful starting point, but must be supplemented by performance and international dimensions of legitimacy. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "international recognition".
items.answer: Acceptance by other states and international organizations of a government as the rightful representative of a state
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: acceptance by other states and international organizations of a government as the rightful representative of a state. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that if most foreign governments recognise a regime, it must be legitimate in the eyes of its people. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: International recognition and domestic legitimacy differ: recognised governments can lack popular support (e.g. Belarus), while unrecognised ones may have it (Somaliland).
items.markingKey: International recognition and domestic legitimacy differ: recognised governments can lack popular support (e.g. Belarus), while unrecognised ones may have it (Somaliland). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between output legitimacy and input legitimacy.
items.answer: Input legitimacy comes from the process – participation, representation, elections; output legitimacy comes from results – effective problem-solving and public goods.
items.markingKey: Input legitimacy comes from the process – participation, representation, elections; output legitimacy comes from results – effective problem-solving and public goods. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify three sources of legitimacy that a government in a parliamentary democracy can draw on, with an example of each.
items.answer: Electoral (winning a free election), legal-rational (constitution, courts), performance (economic management), international recognition (UN membership), traditional (a constitutional monarch as head of state). 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: Electoral (winning a free election), legal-rational (constitution, courts), performance (economic management), international recognition (UN membership), traditional (a constitutional monarch as head of state). 1 mark each.

items.stem: With reference to China's zero-COVID protests in November 2022, explain how it illustrates the fragility of performance legitimacy.
items.answer: After a deadly fire in Urumqi, protests broke out in several Chinese cities; within weeks the government abandoned the zero-COVID policy. when policy outcomes caused hardship, public acceptance weakened, and the regime adjusted to protect its legitimacy
items.markingKey: Context (After a deadly fire in Urumqi, protests broke out in several Chinese cities; within weeks the government abandoned the zero-COVID policy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: when policy outcomes caused hardship, public acceptance weakened, and the regime adjusted to protect its legitimacy – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the fragility of performance legitimacy.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that free and fair elections are the most important source of a regime's legitimacy.
items.answer: Elections are the strongest procedural basis in democratic thought, but in practice legitimacy is sustained by a combination of procedures, performance and recognition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: consent of the governed (Locke, Beetham); peaceful transfer of power; international norms of democracy. Arguments against: performance legitimacy sustains China and Gulf states; elections can be manipulated; traditional and religious legitimacy remain important. Supported judgement: Elections are the strongest procedural basis in democratic thought, but in practice legitimacy is sustained by a combination of procedures, performance and recognition.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "output legitimacy".
items.answer: Legitimacy derived from effective policies that solve problems for citizens (Fritz Scharpf)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: legitimacy derived from effective policies that solve problems for citizens (Fritz Scharpf). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between domestic legitimacy and international legitimacy.
items.answer: Domestic legitimacy is acceptance by a regime's own population; international legitimacy is acceptance by other states and IGOs, which may diverge (e.g. Taiwan has domestic legitimacy but limited recognition).
items.markingKey: Domestic legitimacy is acceptance by a regime's own population; international legitimacy is acceptance by other states and IGOs, which may diverge (e.g. Taiwan has domestic legitimacy but limited recognition). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Venezuela's 2019 and 2024 presidential disputes as an example, explain electoral legitimacy versus control.
items.answer: In 2019 around 50 states recognised opposition leader Juan Guaidó as interim president; after the July 2024 election, the opposition published tally sheets suggesting Edmundo González won, while authorities declared Nicolás Maduro the winner. Maduro retained control of state institutions and the military despite widespread rejection of the election results
items.markingKey: Context (In 2019 around 50 states recognised opposition leader Juan Guaidó as interim president; after the July 2024 election, the opposition published tally sheets suggesting Edmundo González won, while authorities declared Nicolás Maduro the winner.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Maduro retained control of state institutions and the military despite widespread rejection of the election results – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to electoral legitimacy versus control.

items.stem: A newly elected government doubles economic growth but restricts media freedom. Using input and output legitimacy, assess the likely effect on its legitimacy.
items.answer: Output legitimacy rises (growth, services), but input legitimacy falls because participation and free debate are curtailed; long-term legitimacy may suffer if growth slows. Balanced assessment needed.
items.markingKey: Output legitimacy rises (growth, services), but input legitimacy falls because participation and free debate are curtailed; long-term legitimacy may suffer if growth slows. Balanced assessment needed.

items.stem: With reference to two specific examples you have studied, evaluate the argument that performance legitimacy is enough to keep authoritarian regimes in power.
items.answer: Performance is important but rarely sufficient; regimes also rely on coercion, nationalism and co-optation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: China's growth record; Singapore's dominant-party stability; Gulf states provide welfare. Arguments against: Arab Spring shows performance failures topple regimes; repression also needed; nationalism and ideology matter. Supported judgement: Performance is important but rarely sufficient; regimes also rely on coercion, nationalism and co-optation. items.stem: Define the term "expertise-based legitimacy".
items.answer: Authority derived from specialist knowledge and impartial information, often claimed by NGOs and technical agencies
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: authority derived from specialist knowledge and impartial information, often claimed by NGOs and technical agencies. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between legitimacy of a government and legitimacy of an NGO.
items.answer: An NGO's legitimacy rests mainly on expertise, moral authority and accountability to donors and members; a government's legitimacy rests on legal authority, consent of citizens (elections) and performance.
items.markingKey: An NGO's legitimacy rests mainly on expertise, moral authority and accountability to donors and members; a government's legitimacy rests on legal authority, consent of citizens (elections) and performance. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the IMF has faced criticism over legitimacy.
items.answer: Voting shares are based on quotas that favour advanced economies, the managing director has traditionally been European, and loan conditions (structural adjustment, austerity) have been imposed on borrowers with limited voice. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Voting shares are based on quotas that favour advanced economies, the managing director has traditionally been European, and loan conditions (structural adjustment, austerity) have been imposed on borrowers with limited voice. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how the creation of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (2015) may be linked to the legitimacy of the IMF and World Bank.
items.answer: Emerging economies, frustrated by under-representation and slow quota reform, created alternative institutions; the AIIB (China-led) signals that existing institutions' legitimacy is contested.
items.markingKey: Emerging economies, frustrated by under-representation and slow quota reform, created alternative institutions; the AIIB (China-led) signals that existing institutions' legitimacy is contested.

items.stem: With reference to Amnesty International's 2022 report on Ukraine, explain how it illustrates the legitimacy of NGOs.
items.answer: An Amnesty report accused Ukrainian forces of endangering civilians by basing in residential areas; after strong criticism, Amnesty expressed regret for the distress caused and commissioned an external review. the controversy showed that NGO legitimacy depends on perceived impartiality and methodology, and can be contested even when intentions are humanitarian
items.markingKey: Context (An Amnesty report accused Ukrainian forces of endangering civilians by basing in residential areas; after strong criticism, Amnesty expressed regret for the distress caused and commissioned an external review.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the controversy showed that NGO legitimacy depends on perceived impartiality and methodology, and can be contested even when intentions are humanitarian – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the legitimacy of NGOs.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A Council in which Africa, with 54 states, has no permanent seat, while Europe has two, cannot claim to speak for the world."
— Speech by an African head of state at the UN General Assembly, 2023 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, why the legitimacy of the Security Council is challenged.
items.answer: The source argues that the Council is unrepresentative: Africa's many states lack permanent representation while Europe (France, UK) has two seats, so its decisions lack input legitimacy.
items.markingKey: The source argues that the Council is unrepresentative: Africa's many states lack permanent representation while Europe (France, UK) has two seats, so its decisions lack input legitimacy. items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "G4".
items.answer: The group of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan that campaigns for permanent seats on a reformed UN Security Council
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the group of Brazil, Germany, India and Japan that campaigns for permanent seats on a reformed UN Security Council. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly.
items.answer: The Security Council has 15 members, five permanent with veto, and can pass binding resolutions on peace and security; the General Assembly includes all 193 members with one vote each but its resolutions are generally non-binding.
items.markingKey: The Security Council has 15 members, five permanent with veto, and can pass binding resolutions on peace and security; the General Assembly includes all 193 members with one vote each but its resolutions are generally non-binding. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Votes in the IMF are allocated equally, one per member state." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: IMF votes are weighted mainly by quotas based on economic size, plus small basic votes; the US has about 16% and many small states far less than 1%.
items.markingKey: IMF votes are weighted mainly by quotas based on economic size, plus small basic votes; the US has about 16% and many small states far less than 1%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Propose two reforms that could increase the legitimacy of the UN Security Council and explain one obstacle to each.
items.answer: E.g. adding permanent seats for Africa/India/Brazil (obstacle: regional rivals – the Uniting for Consensus group; P5 must ratify under Art. 108); limiting the veto in mass-atrocity situations (France–Mexico initiative; obstacle: Russia, China and the US oppose binding restrictions). 2 marks each.
items.markingKey: E.g. adding permanent seats for Africa/India/Brazil (obstacle: regional rivals – the Uniting for Consensus group; P5 must ratify under Art. 108); limiting the veto in mass-atrocity situations (France–Mexico initiative; obstacle: Russia, China and the US oppose binding restrictions). 2 marks each.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "authority".
items.answer: Power that is recognised as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: power that is recognised as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A regime in which elections are held but the playing field is tilted so heavily that the incumbent rarely loses (Levitsky and Way)"?
items.answer: competitive authoritarianism
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of competitive authoritarianism.

items.stem: What members sits on the UN Security Council for a two-year term?
items.answer: An elected non-permanent member
items.markingKey: An elected non-permanent member. Ten non-permanent members are elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms.

items.stem: Explain why legitimacy reduces the cost of governing.
items.answer: If people accept rules as rightful, they comply voluntarily; the state needs less surveillance and coercion, making power more stable and efficient.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If people accept rules as rightful, they comply voluntarily; the state needs less surveillance and coercion, making power more stable and efficient. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why performance legitimacy can be fragile.
items.answer: If a regime's claim rests on results, an economic slowdown, corruption scandal or crisis (e.g. COVID-19 lockdown protests in China in 2022) can quickly erode support, because there is no procedural basis to fall back on.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If a regime's claim rests on results, an economic slowdown, corruption scandal or crisis (e.g. COVID-19 lockdown protests in China in 2022) can quickly erode support, because there is no procedural basis to fall back on. items.answer: It has 15 members in total: 5 permanent (China, France, Russia, UK, US) and 10 elected for two-year terms.

items.answer: Recognition gives access to the UN seat, foreign aid, loans, trade and diplomatic support; withholding it (as with the Taliban) isolates a regime and signals it is not considered rightful.

items.stem: Using Beetham's framework, explain one reason why the Myanmar military junta after the 2021 coup lacks legitimacy.
items.answer: Legality: it overturned the 2020 election result unconstitutionally; justifiability: few citizens share the belief that the military should rule; consent: mass protests and the civil disobedience movement show no expressed consent. Any one developed.

items.stem: Using the Taliban's return to power in 2021 as an example, explain the role of international recognition.

items.stem: Using the US vetoes on Gaza ceasefire resolutions (2023–2024) as an example, explain perceptions of selectivity and legitimacy.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Power that is recognised as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised"?
items.answer: authority
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of authority.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "competitive authoritarianism"?
options: A member's financial subscription to the IMF, which largely determines its voting share and access to financing
The right of each of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (China, France, Russia, the UK and the US) to block substantive resolutions
Legitimacy derived from effective policies that solve problems for citizens (Fritz Scharpf)
A regime in which elections are held but the playing field is tilted so heavily that the incumbent rarely loses (Levitsky and Way)
items.answer: A regime in which elections are held but the playing field is tilted so heavily that the incumbent rarely loses (Levitsky and Way)
items.markingKey: D. "competitive authoritarianism" is a regime in which elections are held but the playing field is tilted so heavily that the incumbent rarely loses (Levitsky and Way).

items.stem: Which of the following UN General Assembly resolutions of 2022 requires the Assembly to meet after any veto is cast in the Security Council?
items.answer: Resolution 76/262 (the "veto initiative")
items.markingKey: A. The veto initiative, led by Liechtenstein, increases accountability for veto use.

items.stem: Explain the difference between power and authority.
items.answer: Power is the ability to make others act, including through coercion; authority is power accepted as legitimate, so people comply because they believe they ought to.
items.markingKey: Power is the ability to make others act, including through coercion; authority is power accepted as legitimate, so people comply because they believe they ought to. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Authoritarian regimes have no legitimacy at all." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Authoritarian regimes may enjoy performance legitimacy, nationalist or religious legitimacy; e.g. surveys suggest considerable support for the government in China, though such surveys are hard to verify.
items.markingKey: Authoritarian regimes may enjoy performance legitimacy, nationalist or religious legitimacy; e.g. surveys suggest considerable support for the government in China, though such surveys are hard to verify. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Votes in the IMF are allocated equally, one per member state." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: IMF votes are weighted mainly by quotas based on economic size, plus small basic votes; the US has about 16% and many small states far less than 1%.
items.markingKey: IMF votes are weighted mainly by quotas based on economic size, plus small basic votes; the US has about 16% and many small states far less than 1%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between traditional authority and legal-rational authority.
items.answer: Traditional authority rests on custom and inheritance and belongs to a person or dynasty; legal-rational authority rests on impersonal rules and procedures and belongs to an office.
items.markingKey: Traditional authority rests on custom and inheritance and belongs to a person or dynasty; legal-rational authority rests on impersonal rules and procedures and belongs to an office. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between international legitimacy and domestic legitimacy.
items.answer: Domestic legitimacy is acceptance by a regime's own population; international legitimacy is acceptance by other states and IGOs, which may diverge (e.g. Taiwan has domestic legitimacy but limited recognition).
items.markingKey: Domestic legitimacy is acceptance by a regime's own population; international legitimacy is acceptance by other states and IGOs, which may diverge (e.g. Taiwan has domestic legitimacy but limited recognition). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly.
items.answer: The Security Council has 15 members, five permanent with veto, and can pass binding resolutions on peace and security; the General Assembly includes all 193 members with one vote each but its resolutions are generally non-binding.
items.markingKey: The Security Council has 15 members, five permanent with veto, and can pass binding resolutions on peace and security; the General Assembly includes all 193 members with one vote each but its resolutions are generally non-binding. items.stem: Lars writes: "Charismatic authority only exists in dictatorships." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Democratic leaders can have charismatic authority too, e.g. Barack Obama or Jacinda Ardern; charisma is a basis of authority, not a regime type.
items.markingKey: Democratic leaders can have charismatic authority too, e.g. Barack Obama or Jacinda Ardern; charisma is a basis of authority, not a regime type. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Taliban's return to power in 2021 shows the role of international recognition.
items.answer: The Taliban took Kabul in August 2021; they have imposed restrictions on girls' secondary and university education, and the UN has not accepted their nominee for Afghanistan's seat. effective control has not translated into international legitimacy, partly because of the human rights record
items.markingKey: Context (The Taliban took Kabul in August 2021; they have imposed restrictions on girls' secondary and university education, and the UN has not accepted their nominee for Afghanistan's seat.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to the US vetoes on Gaza ceasefire resolutions (2023–2024), explain how it illustrates perceptions of selectivity and legitimacy.
items.answer: The US vetoed several draft resolutions calling for a ceasefire in Gaza before abstaining on Resolution 2728 in March 2024. critics argued that P5 vetoes protect allies and undermine the Council's claim to act impartially for international peace

items.stem: Ana writes: "A regime that wins elections is automatically legitimate." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Elections confer legitimacy only if they are free and fair and part of wider legal-rational rules; manipulated elections (e.g. Belarus 2020) may be rejected by citizens and other states.
items.markingKey: Elections confer legitimacy only if they are free and fair and part of wider legal-rational rules; manipulated elections (e.g. Belarus 2020) may be rejected by citizens and other states. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "If most foreign governments recognise a regime, it must be legitimate in the eyes of its people." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: International recognition and domestic legitimacy differ: recognised governments can lack popular support (e.g. Belarus), while unrecognised ones may have it (Somaliland).
items.markingKey: International recognition and domestic legitimacy differ: recognised governments can lack popular support (e.g. Belarus), while unrecognised ones may have it (Somaliland). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Russia's veto on Ukraine in February 2022, explain how it illustrates the legitimacy gap between the Security Council and the General Assembly.
items.answer: Russia vetoed a Security Council draft resolution condemning its invasion; the General Assembly then adopted Resolution ES-11/1 by 141 votes to 5. the veto blocked action by the body with legal power, while the more representative Assembly expressed broad international disapproval

items.stem: Classify each leader's main source of authority using Weber: (a) the Emperor of Japan, (b) the President of Finland, (c) Ayatollah Khomeini in 1979.
items.answer: (a) traditional (hereditary, though constitutional); (b) legal-rational; (c) charismatic (with religious-traditional elements). 1 mark each.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Performance legitimacy is enough to keep authoritarian regimes in power."

items.stem: "The UN Security Council has lost its legitimacy." Discuss.
items.answer: Its legitimacy is weakened by unrepresentativeness and veto use, but states still treat it as the source of legal authority, so it is diminished rather than lost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: veto paralysis on Syria, Ukraine, Gaza; 1945 membership unrepresentative; selective intervention. Arguments against: still authorises peacekeeping and sanctions (e.g. DRC, South Sudan); states still seek its approval; no viable alternative. items.stem: To what extent is it true that legal-rational authority is the most stable form of legitimacy?
items.answer: Legal-rational authority is generally most stable over time, but it depends on a culture of respect for rules.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rule-based succession (peaceful transfers of power); not dependent on one person. Arguments against: democratic backsliding shows rules can be eroded (Hungary); traditional monarchies have survived for centuries (Japan, Gulf). items.stem: "Free and fair elections are the most important source of a regime's legitimacy." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Elections are the strongest procedural basis in democratic thought, but in practice legitimacy is sustained by a combination of procedures, performance and recognition.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: consent of the governed (Locke, Beetham); peaceful transfer of power; international norms of democracy. Arguments against: performance legitimacy sustains China and Gulf states; elections can be manipulated; traditional and religious legitimacy remain important.
